newsitem.title: BARBADOS: Clinton, Caribbean leaders to focus on trade.
newsitem.headline: Clinton, Caribbean leaders to focus on trade.

text.p: U.S. President Bill Clinton sits down with Caribbean leaders on Saturday for a summit that will focus on trade, drug-trafficking and law enforcement.
On his final stop of a one-week visit to Latin America, Clinton was expected to emphasise economic issues during the meeting, which has gathered leaders from 17 countries.

"We need to ensure that the galloping global economy does not trample small economies or leave them behind," Clinton told officials at a reception on Friday night at the Barbadian governor's house, a stately, whitewashed colonial building.

U.S. officials said one of Clinton's key aims at the summit, which gathered leaders of the 14-member Caribbean Community (Caricom), Haiti and the Dominican Republic, was to fight a perception Washington had lost interest in the region.

White House spokesman Mike McCurry said that as a result of a number of long-running disputes over trade, drug-trafficking and air safety: "there's been a general sense in the Caribbean that U.S. interest in the Caribbean has drifted somewhat."

He added: "One of the president's principal purposes tomorrow is to reaffirm that the United States is a Carribean nation and that we have a long-standing interest in the economic and the political progress of the Caribbean."
Clinton arrived late on Friday in Barbados, his last stop during a one-week tour of Latin America that took him to Mexico and Costa Rica, where he met Central American leaders.
Many of the issues that came up at the Central American summit are expected to be discussed in Barbados, notably the region's desire for closer trade links with the United States.
A U.S. official said that Clinton would discuss giving the region expanded trade preferences to the U.S. market, chiefly for apparel and leather products.

One topic particular to the Caribbean is a dispute over bananas resulting from a World Trade Organisation decision against a European licensing system that gave preferences to firms that distribute and market bananas from the region.
Countries in the region are worried that as a result of the decision, they may lose their duty-free access to the European Union (EU).

U.S. officials said Clinton would seek to reassure them on this point, saying that the United States does not object to the duty-free access and that he would raise the issue with EU leaders later in May to try to find a "satisfactory outcome."
Caribbean leaders have also said the loss of this market, which represents a major source of export earnings, would cause economic chaos and strengthen the hand of drug traffickers.
Drug-trafficking and law enforcement, perennial topics of discussion between the Caribbean nations and the United States, are also on the summit agenda.

The summit, whose meetings began on Thursday, will conclude after a session on Saturday morning. Clinton, who is staying at the home of Briton Sir Anthony Bamford, was expected to remain in Barbados until Monday, when he returns to Washington.
